lessons.title: Chat, Projects, Research and Artifacts: which to use
lessons.eli5: Think of Claude as an office. Chat is the front desk for quick questions, a Project is your own room with your files on the shelf and a note on the door saying how you like things done, and Research is an assistant sent to the library who reports back with the page numbers. An Artifact is the finished poster you can carry out of the office and hand to someone.
lessons.body:
## Why this is tested

The exam guide describes a minimally qualified candidate who already uses Claude regularly in a professional setting. What it checks is whether you pick the **right feature for the job**. Many wrong answers describe something that would technically work, such as pasting the same brand guide into fifty separate chats. The right answer is the feature built for that need.

## The four features named in the exam guide

| Feature | What it is | Reach for it when... | Not ideal when... |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chat** | A single conversation with Claude | You have a one-off question, a quick draft, or a short brainstorm | You will repeat the same setup (files, tone rules) next week |
| **Projects** | A self-contained workspace with its **own chats, knowledge base (uploaded files) and instructions** | Recurring work on the same material: a client account, a course, a product launch | The task is truly one-off and needs no background |
| **Research** | Claude **searches many sources from different angles** and pulls them into a thorough answer **with citations** | A question needs many sources pulled together and you must be able to check where each claim came from | A quick fact, or a task that only uses text you already pasted |
| **Artifacts** | A **standalone piece of output** (document, code, small interactive tool) that opens beside the chat for editing, reusing and sharing | The output is substantial and self-contained, and you will iterate on it or use it outside the chat | A short answer you will read once |

### Chat
Chat is the default. It is fast, needs no setup and suits most single questions. Its weakness is that each new chat starts without your files and instructions, unless memory or a Project supplies them.

### Projects
A Project keeps **instructions and knowledge together** so you don't repeat yourself. Upload the style guide, the product fact sheet and last quarter's report once, write instructions such as "write for HR managers, plain English, UK spelling", and every chat inside that Project starts with that context. A Project's instructions and knowledge apply **only inside that Project**, so one client's material does not leak into another's. Large knowledge still runs into context limits, so curate what you upload — relevant material beats sheer volume. Sharing with colleagues and other controls vary by plan and admin settings.

### Research
Research is for **investigation**, not quick lookups. It searches many sources, explores different angles, and returns one answer **with citations** you can check. Depending on your plan and settings, it may also reach connected sources such as Google Drive or Gmail when those connectors are enabled. Two cautions:
- Research does far more work than a quick chat, so save it for questions that genuinely need many sources.
- Citations make checking easier, but **you still verify** the claims that matter (Domain 2).

### Artifacts
Claude creates an artifact when the content is significant and self-contained, the kind of thing you will probably edit or reuse outside the chat. Examples: a one-page policy summary, a project timeline, a small interactive tool for a sales team. Artifacts can be shared or published; who controls sharing depends on your plan and admin settings.

## Related features you should recognize

The guide's blueprint names four features, but its study advice also mentions Memory, Skills and Code Execution. Know these in one line each:
- **Memory**: Claude can remember useful context across chats. (Covered in the context-limits lesson.)
- **Skills**: packaged instructions and resources for a recurring task, such as "our quarterly report format".
- **File creation (code execution)**: Claude can create and edit real files, not just text in the chat.
- **Connectors**: link Claude to tools such as Google Drive or Gmail so it can read your work content (Domain 5).

## Worked example: one week of a marketing coordinator

| Situation | Best feature | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "What's a polite way to decline a vendor meeting?" | Chat | One-off, no background needed |
| Writing weekly social posts for one brand, using the same voice guide and product list | Project | Same files and rules every time |
| "What are competitors doing with loyalty programs this year, with sources?" | Research | Many sources, needs citations |
| A campaign brief the manager will edit and forward | Artifact | Standalone, edited and shared |
| The final brief as a document file for the agency | File creation | They need a real file, not chat text |

## How to decide fast

Ask three questions in order:
1. **Will I repeat this setup?** If yes, use a Project.
2. **Does the answer need fresh, multi-source, cited information?** If yes, use Research.
3. **Is the output something I will edit, reuse or share on its own?** If yes, use an Artifact (or a created file if a specific format is required).

If all three answers are no, plain chat is right. Don't over-engineer a quick question.

## Plan and admin differences (product-drift note)

Feature availability changes often and varies by plan and admin settings. On the exam, follow the principle and don't rely on exact plan details or caps. If a scenario says a feature is "not available", the usual fix is to check plan or admin settings rather than to change platforms.
keyTakeaways: Chat for one-off questions and quick drafts; no setup.
Projects keep instructions and knowledge files together for recurring work, and apply only inside that Project.
Research searches many sources and returns a cited answer; reserve it for multi-source questions, not quick lookups.
Artifacts are standalone outputs (documents, code, small tools) you edit, reuse and share.
Skills, memory, file creation and connectors complement these four features.
examTips: Look for the repetition cue ("every week", "same files", "same tone"). That points to a Project.
Look for the cue "many sources, with citations". That points to Research. A single known fact is just chat.
"Will be edited and shared" or "reused outside the chat" points to an Artifact.
The best answer usually uses a built-in feature rather than a manual workaround or switching platforms.
commonTraps: Pasting the same reference documents into every new chat instead of putting them in a Project.
Treating Research citations as proof. They make checking easier, but you still need to check.
Using Research for a simple fact. It does far more work than the job needs.
Assuming instructions in one Project apply to other Projects or to ordinary chats. They don't.

lessons.title: Haiku, Sonnet and Opus: the model tiers
lessons.eli5: Think of three delivery options. Haiku is the bike courier: fastest and cheapest, great for lots of small, simple drops. Sonnet is the van: quick and able to carry most jobs. Opus is the specialist truck: slower and pricier, but it handles the big, tricky loads that others can't.
lessons.body:
## What a "model" is

When you use Claude you are talking to a specific **model**, the AI system that produces the answer. Anthropic offers models in **tiers** (families). Higher tiers handle harder thinking but are slower and cost more. Lower tiers are quicker and cheaper. In the Claude apps you pick a model from the model selector. Which models you see depends on your plan and your organization's settings.

The exam guide names three families: **Haiku, Sonnet and Opus**. Learn the **trade-off**, not the version numbers, because versions change every few months.

## The three tiers

| | **Haiku** | **Sonnet** | **Opus** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Speed | Fastest | Fast | Slower |
| Cost | Lowest | Middle | Higher |
| Strength | Simple, well-defined tasks at volume | Balance of speed and intelligence; strong all-rounder | Hard reasoning, long multi-step work, nuance |
| Typical jobs | Sorting or tagging items, short replies, pulling fields out of text, quick summaries | Everyday drafting, analysis, content creation, data work | Complex strategy or policy analysis, long documents with subtle trade-offs, multi-step projects |

### Haiku: fast and economical
Anthropic describes Haiku as its fastest model. It is meant for real-time and high-volume work. Use it when the task is **clear-cut** and you need many results fast: tagging 300 survey comments by theme, turning meeting notes into a short action list, or producing first-pass labels that a person will then review.

### Sonnet: the balanced default
Sonnet is described as the best mix of speed and intelligence. For most everyday knowledge work it is a sensible place to start: drafting a newsletter, analyzing a spreadsheet export, rewriting a policy for a different audience.

### Opus: the most capable of the three
Opus is for work where **quality of reasoning matters more than speed or cost**: comparing three vendor contracts for hidden risks, building a change-management plan from a dozen stakeholder interviews, or a long analysis where one weak step spoils the result. It is slower and uses more of your budget or usage limits.

## Higher tiers can exist

The lineup changes. At the time of writing, Anthropic's docs list a tier above Opus (Claude Fable 5.1) for the most demanding, long-running work, alongside current Opus, Sonnet and Haiku versions. Don't memorize names or prices. Remember the pattern: **more capable means slower and more expensive, lighter means faster and cheaper.**

For reference only (at the time of writing, API list prices per million input tokens): Haiku 4.5 about $1, Sonnet 5.5 about $2, Opus 5.5 about $4, Fable 5.1 about $10. On a subscription plan you don't pay per message, but heavier models still **use up your usage limits faster**.

## Other differences that can matter

- **Context window**: how much text the model can consider at once. Current Opus and Sonnet models list a much larger window than Haiku 4.5 (at the time of writing, 1M vs 200K tokens on the API). For a very long document set, check that the model can hold it.
- **Knowledge cutoff**: each model learned from data up to a certain date. Older or smaller models may know less about recent events. For anything current, use web search or Research and verify.
- **Same family, different version**: a newer Sonnet can beat an older Opus. Tier names show relative position within one generation and are not a permanent ranking.

## Worked example: an HR team

| Task | Tier | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Classify 500 anonymized exit-survey comments into 8 themes | Haiku | Simple, repeatable, high volume; a person spot-checks a sample |
| Draft a friendly reminder about benefits enrollment | Sonnet (or Haiku) | Everyday writing, low complexity |
| Analyze the themes against the compensation policy and propose three retention strategies with trade-offs | Opus | Multi-step reasoning, nuance, high stakes |

Notice that **one workflow can use more than one tier**: a light model for the bulk work and a stronger model for the judgment step.

## What the exam is really asking

Questions in this area rarely ask "which model is fastest?" as pure trivia. They describe a task and ask which choice **fits**. Read the task for cues:
- Volume, speed and simplicity point to the lighter tier.
- Complexity, nuance and multi-step reasoning point to the most capable tier.
- "Most everyday work, balanced" points to the middle tier.
keyTakeaways: Three tiers: Haiku (fastest, cheapest), Sonnet (balanced), Opus (most capable of the three, slower, costlier).
Pick by the task's needs, not by habit or prestige.
Heavier models use more budget or usage limits, even on subscription plans.
Model lineups and versions change; learn the trade-off, not the version numbers. Higher tiers above Opus can exist.
One workflow can mix tiers: light model for bulk, strong model for judgment.
examTips: Match cue words: "high volume", "simple", "quick" lead to the lighter model; "complex", "nuanced", "multi-step", "high-stakes reasoning" lead to the most capable.
If two answers name models, prefer the one that justifies the choice with the task's requirements.
Don't pick an answer because it names the newest or biggest model.
commonTraps: "Always use the most capable model to be safe": this wastes time and budget on simple work.
"The cheapest model is always best for cost": not if it fails the quality bar and creates rework.
Assuming a tier name is a fixed ranking across generations.
Thinking a model knows recent events without web search or Research.

lessons.title: Matching the model to the task: cost, speed and quality
lessons.eli5: You wouldn't hire a senior lawyer to stamp envelopes, and you wouldn't ask an intern to argue a court case. Picking a Claude model works the same way: match the skill level to the job, then check the result is good enough.
lessons.body:
## The three dials

Every model choice balances three things:

| Dial | Question to ask | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Quality** | How good must the result be, and what happens if it is wrong? | A board briefing has to be excellent; internal tags only need to be mostly right |
| **Speed** | Is someone waiting? How many results are needed and how fast? | A live chat with a colleague vs an overnight batch of summaries |
| **Cost / volume** | How many times will this run? What budget or usage limit applies? | Once a month vs 2,000 times a day |

You can rarely max all three. The skill being tested is **finding the cheapest, fastest option that still meets the quality bar**.

## The two starting strategies

Anthropic's model-selection guidance describes two sensible ways to start:

1. **Efficiency-first**: start with a faster, lower-cost model, test it on real examples, and **move up only if it falls short**. Best for high-volume, straightforward, cost-sensitive or speed-sensitive work.
2. **Capability-first**: start with a strong model on complex work where accuracy matters most, get the result right, then see whether a lighter model or lower effort can keep the quality while cutting cost.

Both strategies share the key step: **test with your real material and compare**. Don't decide from the model's reputation.

## A simple decision path

1. **Define "good enough"** in one sentence (for example: "summaries capture every action item and owner; no invented facts").
2. **Estimate volume and urgency.** Many items or a live user favours lighter models.
3. **Judge complexity.** Multi-step reasoning, subtle trade-offs or ambiguous source material favour stronger models.
4. **Try the lightest plausible model** on 5 to 10 real examples.
5. **Check against your definition.** If it passes, keep it. If it fails, first try better prompts and examples, then move up a tier.
6. **Re-check occasionally.** New model versions arrive, so your choice can change.

## Worked examples (all different from the guide's samples)

| Scenario | Quality need | Speed / volume | Good fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| A school admin tags 1,200 parent emails as "attendance", "transport", "billing" or "other" | Moderate; a person handles "other" | High volume | Lighter model |
| A project manager turns a 40-minute meeting transcript into decisions and owners | Must not miss owners | One-off, someone waiting | Balanced model |
| An operations lead compares three outsourcing proposals against a 30-page requirements list and flags risks | High; errors are expensive | Low volume | Most capable model |
| A comms team writes ten headline variants to A/B test | Moderate; humans pick | Quick | Lighter or balanced model |
| A teacher builds a semester curriculum with prerequisites, pacing and assessment alignment | High; multi-step | One-off | Most capable model |

## Mixing models in one workflow

You don't have to choose one model for everything. A common, efficient pattern:
- A **light model** handles the bulk step (sorting, extracting, first drafts).
- A **strong model** handles the judgment step (synthesis, final recommendations).
- A **person** reviews where the stakes demand it.

Anthropic's docs describe this kind of pairing (lower-cost workers plus a frontier model for hard decisions) as a way to keep most of the work at the lower rate.

## Other levers before switching models

If results disappoint, the model is not always the problem. Check these first:
- **A clearer prompt**: goal, audience, format, examples (Domain 1).
- **Better context**: the right files in a Project instead of a vague request.
- **Effort level**: some Claude plans let you choose a lower effort for routine tasks and a higher one for demanding tasks. Higher effort uses more of your limits.
- **Breaking the task into steps**: smaller steps can let a lighter model succeed.

If none of these works, the right move is usually to **switch to a more capable Claude model**, not to abandon Claude or move to another platform.

## When the choice is not yours to make

Associates work within organizational settings. Admins may restrict which models are available, and some workloads, such as automated pipelines that run thousands of items through the API, belong to Developers or Architects. Recognize when model routing at scale has become a technical build, and escalate it.
keyTakeaways: Balance three dials: quality needed, speed needed, cost and volume.
Aim for the lightest model that reliably meets the quality bar.
Efficiency-first (start light, move up if needed) or capability-first (start strong, optimize down); always test on real examples.
Mix models: light model for bulk steps, strong model for judgment, a human for high stakes.
Before switching models, try a clearer prompt, better context, effort level or task decomposition.
examTips: The correct answer names the trade-off: lighter for high-volume, simple work; most capable for complex reasoning.
Answers that test on real examples before committing are usually stronger than ones that decide by reputation.
Distractors often suggest switching platforms or disabling features; these don't address the trade-off.
commonTraps: "Use the biggest model for everything": it wastes cost and adds delay on routine work.
"Use the cheapest model for everything": it can fail the quality bar on complex work and cost more in rework.
Blaming the model when the prompt or context is the real problem.
Choosing once and never re-checking as models improve.

lessons.title: Context limits: restart, summarize or persist
lessons.eli5: Claude's working memory is like a whiteboard. It is big, but it fills up, and the more is scribbled on it, the harder it is to find the important bits. Sometimes you wipe it clean (restart), sometimes you copy the key points onto a fresh board (summarize), and things you need every day go on a poster on the wall (persist, using a Project or memory).
lessons.body:
## What the context window is

The **context window** is the amount of text Claude can consider at once in one conversation: your messages, Claude's replies, uploaded files and instructions. It is Claude's **working memory** for that chat. Text is measured in **tokens** (small chunks of words), but you only need the idea: it is large, but it is **finite**.

At the time of writing, Anthropic's Help Center lists context windows on paid plans of up to 1M tokens for the newest models, with others at 500K or 200K. The numbers will change. The habits in this lesson won't.

## What goes wrong in long chats

- **Earlier details get less attention.** In a very long conversation, important facts from the start can be overlooked or mixed up with later ones. A bigger window does not guarantee better recall. Anthropic's docs call this effect "context rot".
- **Drift.** After many topic changes, Claude may follow outdated instructions or merge two tasks.
- **Usage limits run down faster.** Every new message is processed together with the conversation so far, so long chats consume more of your limit. Anthropic's Help Center says long conversations that trigger automatic context management use more of the limit.
- **Automatic summarizing.** For users with code execution enabled, Claude automatically summarizes earlier messages when a chat nears the limit (you may see it "organizing its thoughts"). This keeps the chat going, but a summary can lose precise details such as exact figures or wording.

## The three moves

| Move | When | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Restart** | New topic; thread has drifted; Claude repeats old mistakes; you're near your usage limit | Open a fresh chat and give a clean, complete prompt |
| **Summarize** | You need continuity but the chat is long or messy | Ask Claude for a summary of decisions, facts, open questions and the exact figures, check it, then paste it into a new chat |
| **Persist** | You need the same context again and again | Put instructions and reference files in a **Project**; rely on **memory** where enabled; save key outputs as artifacts or files |

### Restart
Restarting is not failure. It is often the fastest fix. A clean chat with a well-built prompt beats correcting a confused thread for the tenth time.

### Summarize and carry forward
A good handoff summary includes:
- the goal and audience;
- decisions made and why;
- key facts **with exact numbers and names** (summaries tend to round or drop them);
- open questions and next steps.

Check the summary before using it. If it has an error, the new chat will start with that error.

### Persist
- **Projects** keep durable instructions and knowledge files. Every new chat in the Project starts with them, so you don't re-paste. On paid plans, when project knowledge nears the context limit, Claude switches to **retrieval (RAG)** and pulls only the relevant passages. Documents uploaded to a Project are cached, so referring to them again counts less against your limits.
- **Memory** (where enabled) lets Claude remember useful topics across chats. You can view, edit or delete memories in settings, **pause** memory (keeps existing ones, adds no new ones) or **reset** it (deletes everything, and cannot be undone). **Each Project has its own memory space**, separate from other Projects. On Team and Enterprise plans, the organization owner controls whether memory is available.
- **Incognito chats** are not saved to chat history or memory. Use them for sensitive one-offs you don't want remembered. They do not replace your organization's data policy (Domain 6).
- **Chat search** (paid plans) lets you ask Claude to find what you discussed in earlier chats, instead of repeating it.

## Worked example: a three-week policy rewrite

An HR partner is rewriting the remote-work policy.
1. **Week 1:** creates a Project, uploads the current policy, the legal checklist and survey results, and adds instructions ("plain English, neutral tone, flag anything legal must review").
2. **Week 2:** after 80 messages, Claude starts reusing a clause she rejected on day two. She asks for a summary of decisions (including the rejected clause and why), checks it, and **starts a new chat in the same Project** with it.
3. **Week 3:** she switches to drafting the FAQ, a new task, so she **restarts** with a fresh chat. The Project still supplies the files and rules.

## Quick diagnosis table

| Symptom | Likely cause | Best move |
|---|---|---|
| Claude "forgets" a rule you gave at the start of a long chat | Long context, drift | Summarize and restart, or put the rule in Project instructions |
| You paste the same brand guide every Monday | No persistence | Project knowledge plus instructions |
| A chat about budgets is now about hiring | Topic change | Restart |
| You hit your usage limit quickly | Long thread, heavy attachments, many tools | Fresh chat; Project knowledge; turn off unneeded connectors |
| Claude refers to another client's details | Shared context | Use separate Projects (each has its own memory); review memory |
keyTakeaways: The context window is Claude's working memory for a chat: large but finite.
Long chats can lose earlier details, drift, and use limits faster. A bigger window is not perfect recall.
Restart for new topics or drift; summarize (with exact facts) to carry continuity forward; persist with Projects and memory.
Projects hold durable instructions and files and switch to retrieval (RAG) on paid plans when knowledge gets large.
Memory can be viewed, edited, paused or reset; each Project has separate memory; incognito chats aren't remembered.
examTips: A long, drifting chat calls for a fresh start with a summary, not more corrections in the same thread.
Repeated setup across chats points to a Project, not a longer chat.
When a choice involves sensitive one-off content and memory, consider incognito, but organizational policy still comes first.
commonTraps: Thinking a bigger context window means Claude never misses details.
Carrying a summary forward without checking it. Summaries can drop exact numbers.
Using one giant chat for several unrelated projects.
Believing "tell Claude to forget this" is a data-protection control. Use incognito, memory settings and policy instead.

lessons.title: Selection drill: feature, model and context
lessons.eli5: This is practice for spotting the clue in a question. Each workplace story hides a hint, like "every week", "thousands of", "needs sources" or "the chat is getting long", that tells you which Claude feature or model fits best.
lessons.body:
## How Domain 3 questions are built

Domain 3 is 12% of the exam (about 7 questions). The questions are short workplace stories. Each one contains a **cue** that maps to a feature, a model tier or a context move. Distractors fall into four families:

| Distractor family | What it looks like | Why it's wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **Overkill** | "Use the most capable model for everything" | Ignores cost and speed |
| **Underkill** | "Use the cheapest model for the legal risk analysis" | Ignores the quality bar |
| **Workaround** | "Paste the files into every chat", "keep one huge chat forever" | A built-in feature solves it |
| **Escape hatch** | "Switch platforms", "turn off all features", "stop using AI" | Doesn't address the trade-off |

## The elimination funnel

1. **Find the cue.** Underline the words about repetition, sources, volume, complexity or conversation length.
2. **Remove escape hatches.** Answers that abandon the task or switch platforms are almost never correct.
3. **Remove overkill or underkill.** Check whether the model matches the stakes and volume.
4. **Prefer built-in features over manual workarounds.**
5. **Among what's left, choose the most proportionate option**: the smallest change that fully meets the need.

## Cue map

| Cue in the question | Points to |
|---|---|
| "every week", "same documents", "consistent tone across chats" | Project with instructions and knowledge |
| "multiple sources", "with citations", "current landscape" | Research (then verify key claims) |
| "will edit, reuse and share", "standalone document or tool" | Artifact (or a created file if a format such as .docx is required) |
| "thousands of", "simple", "fast turnaround" | Lighter model (Haiku tier) |
| "nuanced", "multi-step reasoning", "high-stakes analysis" | Most capable model (Opus tier or above) |
| "everyday drafting and analysis" | Balanced model (Sonnet tier) |
| "long chat", "forgot earlier instruction", "drifted" | Summarize and restart, or persist the rule in a Project |
| "don't want this remembered" | Incognito chat or memory settings, within policy |

## Practice stories (original; answers below)

1. **A training coordinator** runs a monthly onboarding workshop and rebuilds the same agenda, slide notes and FAQ from the same three handbooks every time. What should she set up?
2. **A non-profit analyst** must brief the board on how peer organizations fund youth programs, and the board wants to see sources. What feature?
3. **A support operations lead** wants first-pass category labels on 5,000 anonymized tickets by tomorrow, with a person spot-checking a sample. Which model tier?
4. **A strategy manager** needs to weigh three market-entry options against regulatory, staffing and financial constraints described across 12 documents. Which model tier?
5. **A project manager's** chat has run for two days across scope, budget and hiring. Claude is now quoting an old budget figure. What should he do?
6. **A communications officer** drafts a crisis-response checklist that the team will edit and reuse. What output form?

## Answers and reasoning

1. **A Project** with the handbooks as knowledge and instructions for the format. *Trap*: one very long chat, or re-uploading every month.
2. **Research**, then verify the key figures against the cited sources before the board sees them. *Trap*: a plain chat answer from the model's training data, which may be out of date and has no sources.
3. **The lighter, faster tier.** The task is simple and high-volume, and a person checks a sample. *Trap*: the most capable model "for accuracy". It is slower and costlier, and the spot check already covers the risk.
4. **The most capable tier.** Multi-document, multi-factor reasoning with real stakes. *Trap*: the cheapest model "to save budget".
5. **Ask for a summary** of current decisions with the correct figures, check it, and **start a fresh chat** (ideally inside a Project holding the budget file). *Trap*: keep correcting in the same thread.
6. **An Artifact** (or a created document file if the team needs a specific format). *Trap*: leave it as a long inline reply that people must copy and paste.

## Multi-response pattern

Some items say "choose two". For context questions, a typical correct pair is **"summarize the key decisions"** plus **"start a new conversation (in the Project)"**. For model questions, the pair is often **"test on a sample of real items"** plus **"use the lighter model if it meets the bar"**. Read the number required and make sure both choices are independently correct.

## Final check before you answer

- Did I match the **stakes** (quality) and the **volume or speed**?
- Did I choose a **built-in feature** over a manual workaround?
- If verification matters, does my answer still leave room for a **human check**?
keyTakeaways: Every Domain 3 question hides a cue: repetition, sources, volume, complexity or conversation length.
Remove escape hatches first, then overkill and underkill, then manual workarounds.
Proportionate answers win: the smallest change that fully meets the need.
Research and Artifacts still sit inside verification habits from Domain 2.
examTips: Underline the cue words before reading the options.
In "choose two" items, each choice must be correct on its own.
If one option is "switch platforms" or "turn off features", eliminate it immediately.
commonTraps: Picking the most impressive-sounding option (biggest model, most features) instead of the best-fit one.
Choosing a manual workaround when a built-in feature exists.
Forgetting verification after Research because citations are present.
